claimbox · an experiment

xx = y, by fractions

An AI proposes the numbers, claimbox states them as claims, cert-machine decides them.

It began with one picture, xx = 64. The equation has one real root, and no fraction equals it. What a fraction can do is trap it: two fractions on either side, each side one comparison of two whole numbers, decided exactly. This page does that for every y to a thousand, and reads what the fractions show.

the picture

The root of 64, nine decimals decided

x = ln 64 / W(ln 64), where W is Lambert’s function. That form describes the number; it decides nothing. The decimals below are decided by two fractions.

below it
xroot(n) > 458912/135009  CERTIFIED  in 2.9 s
above it
xroot(n) < 400097/117706  CERTIFIED  in 2.3 s
xx grows for x above 1, so x is above a fraction p/q exactly when (p/q)p/q is below 64, that is, when pp is below 64q·qp. No logarithm is evaluated. For the fraction below, each side of that comparison is a whole number of 2,598,236 digits; cert-machine computes both exactly and compares them, given the reduction, which is read and not decided.

458912458912 < 64135009 · 135009458912

The two fractions are neighbouring convergents of the root’s continued fraction [3; 2, 1, 1, 44, 1, 14, 4, 1, 6, …]: the closest fractions for their size, on opposite sides of x. The large 44 is why 758/223 is already within two hundred-thousandths. records/xx64-check.json.

every root

A thousand roots on one curve

Each dot is the root of xx = y. Filled dots are trapped between fractions cert-machine decided; the hollow ones are computed only. The large dots are the roots that are whole numbers.

How tight each trap is

For y up to 100, the bar is the number of decimal places the decided bracket pins down, and the dotted mark is how many the closest fraction with a denominator of at most 1,000 gets right. Full bars are the exact roots.

Every continued fraction, at a glance

Each column is one root, for y from 2 to 400; each row is a partial quotient, the first at the top. The brighter a cell, the larger the quotient. A bright cell means the convergent before it is an unusually good fraction. Near 27 and 256 the bright cells pile up at the top: there, the whole number is the fraction.

what the fractions show

Four things the continued fractions say

Read from the computed roots. The brackets that decide them are cert-machine’s; the patterns are observations, and they are labelled so.

One: only kk has a fraction for a root

The root is a whole number exactly at y = 4, 27, 256 and 3,125, and cert-machine pins each one from both sides: x ≥ k and x ≤ k, both certified. For every other whole y the root is not even algebraic. If it were a fraction p/q that is not whole, xx would be irrational; if it were an irrational algebraic number, xx would be transcendental by the Gelfond–Schneider theorem. A theorem cited, not decided here. So 4 roots are fractions, and every other one is a number no fraction will ever equal.

Two: near kk, one enormous step

Just off kk the root sits just off k, by about 1/(kk(1 + ln k)). Its continued fraction says so with one huge quotient: at y = 255 it is 608, where the slope predicts 610.9; at y = 3,126 it is 8,155, against 8154.5. The closest fraction there is the whole number k, and it is right to three or four decimals.

Three: elsewhere, the roots look like typical numbers

Pool the partial quotients of all the irrational roots and they follow the law that almost every real number obeys: a quotient of 1 occurs 0.41162 of the time, against 0.41504. Their geometric mean is 2.6729, against Khinchin’s constant 2.6855, and (ln qn)/n averages 1.1777, against Lévy’s 1.1866. The roots of xx = y keep no secret pattern in their digits. These are observations on 1,002 computed roots, not a proof.

Four: a few roots have fractions that are almost too good

A large partial quotient makes the convergent just before it unusually close. The largest found is 4,651,670, in the root for y = 709. Its convergent sits closer to the root than any fraction of its size has a right to. For y = 100, the fraction 795/221 is already off by only 4.433289e-08.

how it was done

Proposed, stated, decided

  1. The AI proposeseach root by Newton’s method, its continued fraction, and the fractions that bracket it (tools/xx_study.py). Computed, not trusted.
  2. claimbox stateseach bracket as a claim in its language, xroot(n) > p/q. Its library turns the claim into one exact comparison of whole numbers, and reads y from a pinned file.
  3. cert-machine decideseach comparison from the object alone, as a separate program: CERTIFIED, or REFUTED for the planted wrong brackets.
decided
exact arithmetic by cert-machine, or a count from a record
computed
a number the AI computed; nothing decided it
refused
no mark: ∅ and a word
why these numbers stand as they do
  • A root’s digits are computed. The fractions trapping it are decided, each by one exact comparison.
  • Uniqueness of the root rests on an argument written into the claim: xx ≤ 1 on (0, 1], increasing above 1, and no negative root. cert-machine does not decide that argument.
  • Every number in the text is read from a record, and the page’s build reads it again.

python3 tools/xx_study.py · python3 -m claimbox check corpus/xxy/claims.claim --run · python3 -m claimbox check corpus/xx64/claims.claim --run
